title: Badanekayi yennegai (stuffed brinjal)
sub: brinjal yennagai · ennegayi · badanekai
servingLabel: half the curry; eat with rotti or rice
uses: 1 burner, lidded heavy pan and mixer
keeps: Cook for this meal; refrigerate promptly if saving any.
intro: North Karnataka-style fresh-coconut and onion variant. Peanuts and sesame are essential here; this is not Tamil ennai kathirikai. Sauce water is a starting amount, adjusted by tenderness.

items.name: Small tender purple brinjals
items.note: whole tender baby brinjals; use weight, count varies

stepTemplates: Prepare. Rinse {{brinjal}} brinjals. Cut two crossing slits from the rounded end towards the stalk, keeping the crown joined. Inspect inside; discard damaged fruit. Hold in water while making the paste, then drain and pat dry.
Extract. Soften {{tamarind}} tamarind in {{soak}} warm water for 10 minutes. Squeeze and strain; retain the liquid, discard seeds or fibres.
Roast. In a dry pan on low heat, stir {{peanuts}} peanuts until nutty; roast {{sesame}} sesame separately until fragrant. Cool before grinding.

Grind. Powder the cooled nuts and seeds. Blend with {{coconut}} fresh coconut, {{cumin}} cumin, {{chilli}} chillies, {{ginger}} ginger and {{herb}} coriander, adding {{grind}} water gradually. Stop at a thick, spoonable paste.

Combine. Mix in {{onion}} onion, {{sambar}} sambar powder, {{turmeric}} turmeric, {{jaggery}} jaggery, {{salt}} salt and enough tamarind liquid to keep the stuffing thick. Reserve remaining liquid. Do not taste uncooked spice paste to assess final seasoning.
Stuff. Gently ease paste into each slit without snapping the crown. Retain every spoon of leftover paste for the gravy.
Temper. Heat {{oil}} oil on medium in a heavy lidded pan. Add {{mustard}} mustard; when it crackles, add {{garlic}} garlic and {{leaves}} curry leaves carefully. Lower heat if garlic darkens.

Simmer. Set brinjals in one layer. Turn gently for 2–3 minutes. Add leftover stuffing, reserved tamarind liquid and {{simmer}} water. Cover and simmer gently for about 20–30 minutes; turn and scrape the base every few minutes.

Check. A knife should enter the thick flesh beside the crown easily. If firm or the gravy catches, add a small splash of water and cook longer. Stop when the flesh is soft and the sauce coats it; oil separation alone is not doneness. Adjust seasoning after cooking.

title: Khara pongal (ven pongal)
sub: ghee pongal · savory pongal · ಹುಗ್ಗಿ
uses: 3 L stovetop pressure cooker, burner and small tempering pan
keeps: Cook for this meal; refrigerate promptly if saving any.
intro: A rice-forward, softly mashed pongal. The estimated raw-start time includes natural pressure release and tempering. Confirm pressure-cooker availability before choosing this version.
stepTemplates: Roast and rinse. Pick over {{dal}} dal. Dry-roast on low until fragrant, not brown. Cool briefly; rinse with {{rice}} rice and drain.

Load. Add grains, {{water}} water, {{ginger}} ginger, {{cumin-cook}} cumin, {{hing}} hing and {{salt}} salt to the cooker. Follow its minimum liquid and foaming-food fill limits; never scale past those limits.

Pressure-cook. Close according to the manufacturer. The source gives roughly 11–12 minutes at pressure; cooker and dal age vary. Maintain the cooker’s required operating heat, then turn off. This is not a universal whistle count.
Release. Wait for pressure to fall naturally and the indicator to confirm zero pressure before opening. Allow roughly 10–20 minutes, longer if needed; never force the lid.

Texture. Both grains should mash readily. If still firm, add liquid if needed and cook further using the cooker instructions. Mash lightly; thin thick pongal with hot water until soft and spoonable, not separate like pulao.
Temper. In a small pan heat {{ghee}} ghee. Sizzle {{cumin}} cumin; add {{nuts}} cashews until pale gold, then {{pepper}} pepper and {{leaves}} curry leaves carefully. Stop before spices burn.
Finish. Stir the tempering into the hot grains. Rest loosely covered for 5 minutes; loosen with hot water if it thickens. Serve hot.

title: Kesari Bath (rava sweet)
sub: kesari bhath · rava kesari · sheera
keeps: Cook for this meal; refrigerate promptly if saving any.
intro: A small-portion Karnataka sweet, not a high-protein meal or a weight-loss claim. This version uses the Dassana water/sugar ratio, not the richer Hebbar ratio.

items.name: Saffron
items.note: optional; omit for an uncoloured sweet

stepTemplates: Roast. Stir {{rava}} fine rava in a dry heavy pan on low for about 5–6 minutes, until fragrant without darkening. Transfer to a plate.
Nuts. Melt {{ghee-nut}} ghee in the pan. Fry {{nuts}} cashews until pale gold; lift onto a plate. Keep the ghee in the pan.
Liquid. Add {{water}} water cautiously, then {{sugar}} sugar and {{raisins}} raisins. Add {{saffron}} saffron if using. Stir until dissolved and bring to a gentle boil.
Combine. Reduce heat. Sprinkle in the roasted rava in several additions while stirring continuously with a long-handled spoon. Keep hands and face away from hot splashes.
Cook. Mix in {{ghee-finish}} ghee and {{cardamom}} cardamom. Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 3–4 minutes, stirring to prevent catching.
Check. The granules should be fully swollen with no hard pale centres. If gritty, add a little hot water and cook longer. Fold in the nuts and serve warm; it firms as it cools.

title: Cabbage pakoda (besan fritters)
sub: cabbage pakora · patta gobhi pakode · cabbage bhajiya
servingLabel: half the batch of small fritters
uses: 1 burner, deep frying pan, slotted spoon and oil thermometer
keeps: Cook for this meal; refrigerate promptly if saving any.
intro: Besan-only cabbage fritters. This is a fried snack, not a low-oil recipe. Nutrition assumes 20 g oil absorbed by the whole batch solely for estimation; actual uptake may differ substantially.

items.name: Neutral oil for the pan
items.note: pan quantity, not consumption; actual absorbed oil is unknown

stepTemplates: Prepare. Rinse vegetables and drain thoroughly. Finely shred {{cabbage}} cabbage; chop {{onion}} onion and {{chilli}} chilli. Keep water away from the hot-oil area.
Mix. Combine vegetables with {{besan}} besan, {{ginger}} ginger, {{herb}} coriander, {{turmeric}} turmeric, {{powder}} chilli powder and {{salt}} salt.

Hydrate. Add water a spoon at a time, up to {{water}} initially. Vegetables release moisture, so stop once a thick mixture clings to a spoon. It should drop in small mounds, not pour as a thin batter.
Heat oil. Use {{oil}} as a pan-size guide, enough for frying while keeping the deep pan well below half full. Heat on medium to about 180 °C. Never leave it unattended or add water to oil.
Test. Lower one small spoonful close to the oil surface using a dry spoon. It should rise with steady bubbles. Reduce heat if it darkens before the middle cooks; recheck temperature.

Fry. Add a few small, loose spoonfuls without crowding. Let the coating set, then turn gently. Fry until evenly golden; open the first fritter and check for a cooked, non-pasty centre and tender cabbage.
Finish. Lift with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper. Let oil return to temperature before each batch; total time depends on pan size. Serve hot with a separately prepared chutney.

title: Cheese corn balls
sub: crisp crumb outside, melting cheese inside · air fryer or deep-fried
uses: Air fryer (or a deep pan for frying), mixing bowl, freezer
keeps: Best eaten hot; they turn chewy as they cool. Shaped, coated balls can wait in the freezer until you cook them.
intro: Mashed potato binds sweet corn and cheese into a dough; a cornflour slurry and bread crumbs make the shell that stops the cheese leaking. Chilling before cooking is what keeps them whole.

items.name: Sweet corn kernels, cooked and drained dry
items.note: steam or boil until tender; raw kernels can burst

items.name: Potato, boiled, peeled and mashed smooth
Cheese, grated
items.note: processed cheese holds best; mozzarella melts faster

items.name: Salt
items.note: less than usual; the cheese is salty

items.name: Cornflour, for the slurry
items.note: Hebbar uses half cornflour, half maida

items.name: Panko or dry bread crumbs, for coating
items.note: about 30 g sticks to the balls

stepTemplates: Make the mixture. In a bowl, mash {{potato}} potato with {{corn}} corn, {{cheese}} cheese, {{onion}} onion, {{chilli}} green chilli, {{garlic}} garlic and {{coriander}} coriander. Season with {{flakes}} chilli flakes, {{pepper}} pepper, {{oregano}} oregano and {{salt}} salt.

Bind. Add {{crumbs}} bread crumbs and {{cornflour}} cornflour and mix with your hand until it holds together like soft dough. Sticky or wet? Add a spoon more crumbs. Cracking? Add a few drops of water.
Shape. Wet your palms lightly and roll the mixture into about 10 smooth, lime-sized balls with no cracks. For a bigger melting centre, press a small cube of cheese into each and seal it well.
Coat. Whisk {{slurry}} cornflour with {{water}} water into a thin, smooth slurry. Dip each ball in it, then roll in {{panko}} panko. For a sturdier shell, dip and roll a second time.
Chill (20 min). Freeze the coated balls on a plate for 20 minutes so the cheese is cold when the crust starts to set.

Air fry (10–15 min). Preheat the air fryer to 180 °C. Place the balls in one layer with space between them, brush or spray with {{oil}} oil and cook 10–15 minutes, turning halfway, until golden and crisp. Check the first batch from 10 minutes.

Or deep-fry. Heat oil in a deep pan on medium; a small test piece should rise steadily, not shoot up browning. Fry a few balls at a time, turning gently once the crust has set, until golden. Oil that's too cool lets the cheese escape. Drain on paper.
Serve hot with ketchup or green chutney.

stepTemplates: Cook the corn. Boil or steam {{corn}} corn until tender, drain, and spread it on a plate to steam dry. Wet corn makes soggy sandwiches.

title: Dried green peas masala (vatana curry)

intro: Dried green peas (hara vatana) are cheap, keep for months and give a filling, high-fibre curry. They must be soaked and pressure-cooked; in a pan they take an hour or more.
stepTemplates: Check and rinse. Drain {{peas}} soaked peas, smell them (sour or slimy means discard), and rinse 2–3 times.

Pressure-cook (3–5 whistles). Cook the peas with {{water}} water (to cover by about 2 cm), {{salt1}} salt and {{turmeric1}} turmeric on medium for 3–4 whistles; let the pressure drop on its own. A pea should mash easily between your fingers; if not, cook 1–2 whistles more. Keep the cooking water.
Masala (12 min). Heat {{oil}} oil, add {{cumin}} cumin, then {{onion}} onion and fry until golden, 6–8 minutes. Add {{ggarlic}} garlic, {{gginger}} ginger and {{gch}} green chilli for 1 minute.
Tomatoes (5 min). Add {{tomato}} tomatoes, {{turmeric}} turmeric, {{chillip}} chilli powder, {{corp}} coriander powder and {{salt2}} salt; cook until soft and the oil starts to separate.
Simmer (10 min). Add the peas with enough cooking water for a thick gravy and simmer 8–10 minutes. Mash a ladleful against the pan to thicken.
Finish with {{garam}} garam masala, {{coriander}} coriander and {{lemon}} lemon juice.

tips.title: Taste a raw piece first
tips.text: Bottle gourd should taste bland. If a raw piece tastes even slightly bitter, spit it out and throw the whole gourd away: the bitter compound (cucurbitacin) is toxic and cooking does not destroy it.

tips.title: Choosing and cutting
tips.text: Pick a firm, light-green gourd with smooth skin that a fingernail dents easily. Peel, halve, and scoop out the seeds only if they are large and hard.

tips.title: Unsoaked dal
tips.text: Without soaking, the dal needs more whistles and the gourd turns to mush; cook the dal 2 whistles first, then add the gourd for 1–2 more.

stepTemplates: Soak and check. Rinse {{dal}} chana dal and soak 30 minutes. Peel the gourd and taste a tiny raw piece: if it is bitter at all, discard the whole gourd. Cube {{lauki}} bottle gourd.

Masala (8 min). Heat {{oil}} oil in the cooker; add {{cumin}} cumin and {{hing}} hing, then {{onion}} onion until light golden. Add {{ginger}} ginger, {{garlic}} garlic and {{gch}} green chilli for a minute.
Tomatoes (5 min). Add {{tomato}} tomatoes, {{turmeric}} turmeric, {{chillip}} chilli powder and {{corp}} coriander powder; cook until soft and the oil separates.

Pressure-cook (3–4 whistles). Add the drained dal, the gourd, {{salt}} salt and {{water}} water; stir and cook 3–4 whistles on medium. Let the pressure drop on its own. The dal should be soft but whole; the gourd releases water, so don't add more at first.
Finish. Simmer open for 2–3 minutes to adjust thickness, then add {{garam}} garam masala, {{coriander}} coriander and {{lemon}} lemon.

tips.text: Bottle gourd should taste bland. If a raw piece tastes even slightly bitter, spit it out and throw the whole gourd away: the bitter compound (cucurbitacin) is toxic and cooking does not destroy it.

title: Sorekai huli (bottle gourd sambar)
sub: Karnataka-style toor dal and bottle gourd huli · rice
keeps: Fridge 2–3 days; reheat until boiling.
intro: Bottle gourd is ideal for huli: it soaks up the tamarind, sambar powder and coconut. Cook the dal and gourd in the cooker, then boil everything together.
stepTemplates: Check the gourd. Peel and taste a tiny raw piece of the gourd; if it is bitter at all, throw the whole gourd away. Cube {{lauki}} bottle gourd.

Cook dal and gourd (3 whistles). Put {{toor}} toor dal with half the {{water}} water and {{turmeric}} turmeric in the cooker; set the gourd in a separate bowl on top (or straight in with the dal) and cook 3 whistles. Let the pressure drop; mash the dal.

Boil the huli (10 min). Boil the gourd with {{tamarind}} tamarind, {{sambar}} sambar powder, {{jaggery}} jaggery, {{salt}} salt and {{coconut}} coconut (ground with a little water, if using) for 5 minutes, until the raw tamarind smell goes. Add the mashed dal and the rest of the water for a pourable huli and boil 3–4 minutes more.
Temper. Heat {{oil}} oil; add {{mustard}} mustard, then {{hing}} hing, {{redch}} red chilli and {{curry}} curry leaves; pour over the huli and add {{coriander}} coriander.

title: Aloo kalonji (potatoes with nigella seeds)
sub: dry potato sabzi where kalonji is the star · rotis, puris or dal-rice

intro: A simple dry potato dish flavoured mainly with kalonji. Mustard oil is traditional in eastern India; any oil works.

items.name: Potatoes, peeled and cut in small cubes
Oil (or mustard oil, heated till it smokes lightly, then cooled a little)

stepTemplates: Cut. Cut {{potato}} potatoes into small, even cubes (about 1.5 cm) so they cook through in the pan; keep them in water until you start, then drain well.
Kalonji (30 sec). Heat {{oil}} oil on medium, add {{kalonji}} kalonji and let it sizzle until fragrant — don't let it burn. Add {{gch}} green chillies.

Cook the potatoes (15–18 min). Add the potatoes, {{turmeric}} turmeric, {{chillip}} chilli powder and {{salt}} salt; toss, cover and cook on low-medium, stirring every few minutes, until a cube crushes easily. Sprinkle a spoon of water if they stick.
Crisp and finish (3 min). Uncover and fry 2–3 minutes for crisp edges; add {{amchur}} amchur and {{coriander}} coriander.

title: Jolada rotti (jowar roti)
sub: North Karnataka staple flatbread · hot-water dough, no oil
uses: Tawa, rolling pin or palms, 1 burner
keeps: Soft rotis are best fresh; dried-out (kadak) rotis keep for days in a closed tin.
intro: Jowar has no gluten, so the dough is made with hot water and kneaded until smooth, and each roti is patted or rolled on a well-floured surface. It takes a few tries; a rolling pin is fine.

items.name: Hot water
items.q: about ¾ cup / 180 ml, as needed

stepTemplates: Dough (5 min). Mix {{jowar}} jowar flour and {{salt}} salt; pour in {{water}} hot (just-boiled) water a little at a time and mix with a spoon. When cool enough to touch, knead with the heel of your hand for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, soft dough with no cracks. Knead only what you'll roll in the next few minutes; it dries quickly.

Shape. Take a lemon-sized ball, knead it again briefly, and flatten on a board dusted with {{dust}} jowar flour. Roll or pat into a 6–7 inch circle, turning it often and dusting under it so it doesn't stick. Mend edge cracks with a wet finger.
Tawa. Lift the rotti carefully onto a hot tawa, floured side up. Spread a little water over the top with your fingers.

Cook (3–4 min). When the water dries (about 1 minute), flip and cook the other side until brown spots appear. Puff it directly on the flame or press with a cloth on the tawa. Stack in a cloth-lined box.

title: Sabudana khichdi (non-sticky)
sub: soaked sago with peanuts and potato · breakfast or fasting days
keeps: Best hot; it turns chewy as it cools.
intro: Everything depends on the soak: rinse the starch off, soak with water just level with the pearls, and drain completely. Then cook only until the pearls turn translucent.

items.name: Water, for soaking
items.q: just enough to cover, about ¾ cup

stepTemplates: Rinse and soak (4–8 h). Rinse {{sabudana}} sabudana 3–4 times, rubbing gently, until the water is fairly clear. Soak with {{water}} water just level with the pearls (not more), covered, 4–6 hours or overnight depending on the brand.

Test and drain. A pearl should squash easily between your fingers with no hard white centre. Drain in a colander for 15 minutes so no water remains. Mix in {{peanuts}} crushed peanuts, {{salt}} salt and {{sugar}} sugar — the peanut powder keeps the pearls separate.
Temper (2 min). Heat {{ghee}} ghee in a non-stick pan; add {{cumin}} cumin, {{gch}} green chillies and {{curry}} curry leaves, then {{potato}} potato and fry 1 minute.

Cook (5–7 min). Add the sabudana and toss gently on low-medium heat until most pearls turn translucent. Stop then — overcooking makes it gummy. Finish with {{lemon}} lemon and {{coriander}} coriander.

title: Shavige uppittu (vermicelli upma)
sub: Karnataka breakfast · 15 minutes
keeps: Best fresh; packs for a lunch box the same day.
intro: Roasted vermicelli cooked in a seasoned onion-vegetable base. Wheat vermicelli is roasted first; rice vermicelli is soaked or boiled briefly instead (follow the packet).
stepTemplates: Roast (4 min). Dry-roast or roast {{shavige}} vermicelli in a teaspoon of the oil, stirring, until light golden. Set aside. (Skip if the packet says pre-roasted.)

Temper (3 min). Heat the rest of {{oil}} oil; add {{mustard}} mustard, then {{uraddal}} urad dal, {{chanadal}} chana dal and {{peanuts}} peanuts until golden. Add {{curry}} curry leaves, {{gch}} green chillies, {{ginger}} ginger, {{onion}} onion and {{veg}} carrot or peas; cook until the onion softens.

Boil, then add vermicelli. Pour in {{water}} water and {{salt}} salt and bring to a full boil. Only then add the vermicelli, stir once, cover and cook on low 4–5 minutes until the water is absorbed and the strands are soft.

Rest and finish. Turn off the heat, keep covered 2 minutes, then fluff with a fork and mix in {{coconut}} coconut, {{lemon}} lemon juice and {{coriander}} coriander. Don't overcook or it turns sticky.

items.name: Fresh methi leaves, picked, washed and finely chopped

stepTemplates: Dough (8 min). Mix {{atta}} atta, {{besan}} besan, {{methi}} methi, {{curd}} curd, {{ginger}} ginger, {{gch}} chilli, {{turmeric}} turmeric, {{chillip}} chilli powder, {{ajwain}} ajwain, {{salt}} salt and {{oil1}} oil. title: Heerekai palya (North Karnataka ridge gourd curry)
sub: ridge gourd in a ground onion-coconut masala · jolada rotti, chapati or rice
keeps: Fridge 2 days.
intro: Ridge gourd soaks up a spicy ground masala and turns soft but holds its shape. Peel only the sharp ridges, not all the green skin.

items.name: Ridge gourd, ridges peeled, cut in 2-inch pieces

stepTemplates: Prep. Peel just the hard ridges off {{gourd}} ridge gourd, taste a raw piece (throw it away if bitter), and cut into 2-inch lengths.
Grind. Blend {{onion1}} onion, {{coconut}} coconut, {{sambar}} sambar powder, {{garlic}} garlic and {{tomato}} tomato with {{water1}} water into a smooth paste.
Temper and sauté (5 min). Heat {{oil}} oil; add {{mustard}} mustard, {{cumin}} cumin and {{curry}} curry leaves, then the gourd and {{turmeric}} turmeric; sauté until it starts to soften.

Cook (12–15 min). Add the paste and fry until the raw smell goes, then add {{salt}} salt, {{jaggery}} jaggery and {{water2}} water. Cover and cook on low, stirring once or twice, until the gourd is soft but still holds its shape. Finish with {{coriander}} coriander.

title: Hagalakai gojju (sweet-sour bitter gourd)
sub: bitter gourd tamed with salt, tamarind and jaggery · rice or chapati
keeps: Fridge 4–5 days; the flavour improves.
intro: Thin slices are salted to draw out bitterness, squeezed, fried, then simmered in tamarind and jaggery. Even people who avoid karela usually like it.

items.name: Bitter gourd, thinly sliced (seeds removed if large)
Salt
items.note: taste first; the gourd keeps some salt

stepTemplates: Salt (20 min). Toss {{bg}} sliced bitter gourd with {{salt1}} salt and {{turmeric}} turmeric; leave 20 minutes. Squeeze hard, rinse once in water and squeeze again — this removes much of the bitterness.

Fry (8–10 min). Heat {{oil}} oil; add {{mustard}} mustard, {{hing}} hing and {{curry}} curry leaves, then the squeezed slices. Fry on medium until they shrink and brown at the edges; the more you fry, the less bitter.
Simmer (8 min). Add {{tamarind}} tamarind with {{water}} water, {{jaggery}} jaggery, {{rasam}} rasam powder and {{salt2}} salt; simmer until thick and glossy. Stir in {{sesame}} sesame powder.
